speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today our Frenchspeaking fellow Canadians throughout Canada are rejoicing for they are celebrating St. John the Baptist day, in honour of their patron saint.
Even if members of this house do not all share in the same traditions, I am sure, however, that all of them will join me in tendering to our French-speaking colleagues and to all French Canadians of this country our best wishes on this festive occasion.
The elements of the Canadian nationality are many and not easily definable. It is generally recognized, however, that one of the features of our nationality is the free association, over a period of two centuries, of two cultures, two traditions, for the achievement of one great Canada.
It is fitting that each year our Frenchspeaking fellow citizens relive the finest pages of their history, which is the history of all Canada, since their gallant forebears extended their activity to the furthermost reaches of our country.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to table two copies of a report by the national energy board on two applications for licences to export gas to the United States. Both these applications involve small volumes of gas and both, in effect, represent renewals or extensions of existing export licences.
The Canadian-Montana Pipe Line Company has been exporting gas from Alberta to the state of Montana since 1952. The existing licence expires September 1, 1960. The new licence applied for would terminate on May 14, 1974, the same date on which its Alberta permit and the federal power commission permit to the Montana Power Company to import gas into the United States expire.
The national energy board found that the total quantity of gas proposed to be exported exceeded the established reserves for the fields from which the gas would be removed, and accordingly reduced the total quantity of gas which the applicant might export over the period of the new licence from some 268 billion cubic feet to 190 billion cubic feet.
The second application, that of Gordon Plotke, is for a five year licence, and the maximum annual volume of gas to be exported is only 10 million cubic feet. This is a local matter involving the gas from one well only, and gas which is not considered saleable other than in this particular export.
In its report the board indicates that it is prepared to issue export licences to the Canadian-Montana Pipe Line Company and to Gordon M. Plotke. The government concurs with the board's findings on these applications, and accordingly will authorize the issue of the licences on the terms set forth in the report.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. The commissioner has announced this morning that there has been a change in the long-standing marriage regulations. Under the new regulations a member of the force may be permitted to marry if he is at least 21 years of age and has served in the force in a satisfactory manner for two years. Formerly the regulations required that a member serve satisfactorily for five years before marriage, with one or two exceptions.
The original intent of the rather stringent regulations was to ensure maximum mobility in the service by having at all times a 50 per cent strength of single men. This arrangement is no longer considered necessary and, in fact, the married strength of the force now exceeds this figure. The commissioner is of the opinion that the change in regulations will be welcomed by many young men already in the force, and will also remove an obstacle to recruiting those young men otherwise suitable who regarded the marriage regulations with disfavour. I concur in that opinion.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at ten o'clock last night I was discussing the importance of the work of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys with regard to the exhaustion of our reserves of minerals. The rate of consumption of any mineral resource is subject to many factors. Under any system of free enterprise, mineral deposits are normally exploited only when the margin between costs of production and the price to the consumer will yield a profit to the operator. Obviously, therefore, any improvements in mining, milling or refining techniques that result in lower production costs or an increase in the percentage of the metal recovered will correspondingly increase the total of our commercially available resources. The more efficient we become in the utilization of low grade ores, the more satisfactory our supply position. The same results can also be obtained in the free market when the consumer is willing or able to pay increased prices.
The part that this department should have been playing in technological research is, I think, abundantly clear and has been for a long time. It is essential that this work
5362	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys now go ahead. No less important is the essential work required in the field of conservation. I find it most significant that in the cases of agriculture, forestry, fisheries and certain other fields of resources development, some progress has been made in the direction of conservation. All these are renewable resources. Yet in the case of minerals, which are not renewable, there has been practically no effort, except in time of war, to interfere with the free play of a market that is interested primarily in profits. This is an anomaly that cannot continue forever. So we have several reasons for being concerned about the mineral resource future of Canada.
Well, what should this department be doing now as well as for future generations? Our hopes for the future, in my view, should be directed first toward the discovery of new ore bodies. There is certainly ample scope in Canada for such activities today. The greatest hope for fresh supplies of ore depends upon the discovery of new ore bodies in those areas of Canada yet undeveloped. Here I cannot help but draw the attention of this committee to the vast areas of the north where such activities have a very wide scope.
The second step to be taken in our effort to meet the undoubted future demands which will be placed on our mineral resources and to forestal shortages at home is the improvement of our techniques of extraction and processing. New and more efficient methods of mining are constantly being sought. In addition, we must broaden the field of research in our metallurgical practices. The record of discovery in this field offers good evidence that further research will result in further refinements. In the future, as higher grades of ore are depleted, more attention must be given to the treatment of complex and low grade ore bodies by leaching or other chemical methods. Further study should also be given to the possibility of obtaining minerals from sea water.
Finally, in addition to the search for new ore bodies and the improvement of our processes of extraction and treatment, greater study must be given to the possibilities of conservation and substitution.
Now, Mr. Chairman, how is the department to meet the demands which are being placed upon it now and in the future should the course which I have advocated be implemented? The evidence before the committee on mines, forests and waters last year clearly indicated an extremely complicated general administration of the diversified activities of this department. There are many factors which contribute to this situation; the nature of the operations of the various branches of


the department; the large number of individual projects conducted under mobile and remote conditions; the operation of a fleet of ships and launches; the operation of a large number of fixed and rotary wing charter aircraft; the operation of a fleet of about 225 motor vehicles and railway speeders, tracked vehicles, dog teams, horses and the like; and large scientific laboratories in Ottawa. No wonder, then, that procurement, supply, maintenance and financing are difficult tasks, and it will-it must-get even more difficult as the volume of field operations increase and as they progressively move to more outlying areas of the country. The problem of logistics must become more acute.
The department must be allowed to relieve the scientific and technical staff of the administrative requirements associated with their work, and to the maximum degree possible. An accelerated effort toward this objective should be immediately undertaken by the provision of the necessary staff. It is abundantly clear that the growth of the functional operations of the department over many years has not been matched by a corresponding growth in administrative assistance.
The functional operations of the department are hampered by unduly restrictive policies of financial administration. The policy now requires treasury board approval to be given to a very considerable number of individual financial proposals. The department's job could be made much easier and more efficient by enlarging the authority of the minister to meet these flexible demands. As the department expands its activities generally an increased administrative activity will require staff additions if the department is to attain any degree of efficiency.
The most serious difficulty facing the department in the solution of its problems is the recruiting and retention of capable technical and scientific staff. No organization can maintain a high order of research productivity without a high percentage of creative personnel. An organization such as the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is only as productive as the quality of its staff. To me it is simply amazing that the staff in the number existing in this department for many years has produced such a quality of work, which has allowed Canada to maintain at least a tenuous position in this field.
The department is recruiting and operating in a professional field where the competition for staff reaches its highest intensity. This competition comes from industry in both Canada and the United States, and more recently from the universities. Even junior staff is now being attracted to the secondary

schools. Competition for staff begins at the recruiting stage, where salary levels are slightly less than those of crown organizations such as the national research council and the defence research board and much less than in industry, through to the more senior and specialist grades, where salaries in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys are much below those offered elsewhere, often to the extent of between $3,000 and $4,000. This situation hurts the organization now and affects the future operations of the department itself and consequently the future of the mineral industry and the future of Canada.
A proportion of highly capable young men must be recruited to assure the future efficiency of any research organization. There is no substitute for intelligence and ability in a research organization. What possibly presents a more serious situation is staff who have become national or international specialists in research areas, and who are attracted away when they are most productive by offers of salaries which are far beyond what the department can pay.
I understand that the purpose of the department is to encourage the mining industry in every way possible, and in keeping with this policy I do not feel that we should mind losing some of our staff to Canadian industry. In fact I think we would welcome and encourage a healthy interchange of staff with Canadian industry. What really hurts, however, is when we lose highly trained specialists to the United States. A specialist takes 10 to 15 years to reach his maximum usefulness, and this may represent $100,000 in training costs. The loss of these highly trained engineers and scientists presents a serious national problem. A high percentage of our specialists who leave go to the United States. It might be of interest to note here that the Financial Post of May 2, 1959 stated that 1,200 Canadian engineers settled in the United States during 1958.
If the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is to maintain a staff capable of meeting the national demands, salaries must be raised to a competitive level. This is most important at the senior engineer and scientist level. I understand that in recent years the personnel establishments of the various divisions of the department have been fixed by yearly meetings between treasury board, the civil service commission and the department, and that for the 18 months following this meeting there is little elasticity for changing staff about to meet new demands or altering situations. This presents a most difficult problem, since extraordinary demands, which are being continually presented, follow no
24, 1960	5363
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys established pattern. The result is a measure of inefficiency and administration confusion. A department such as mines and technical surveys, which must meet unexpected demands, should have more flexibility in the recruitment and use of its staff. The rigid formula now applied is fraught with difficulties, and efficiency suffers.
These steps require to be taken now. They should have been taken many years ago. If we fail to act now, future generations of Canadians will have to bear the consequences of our blindness; and our responsibility for failing, with full knowledge of the facts, to take the necessary measures, will be heavy in their sight.

One of the bright spots in the economy of British Columbia at present is the tremendous increase in interest and investment in metal mining. I was on the coast a few weeks ago and took the opportunity to drop into the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines office. While I was there it was obvious that it was a most active place. There were a number of people there from various parts of the United States and other parts of the world, and the manager of the bureau informed me that they had received make grants to such organizations as this, but ever before in their history. I know that to date it is not the policy of the department to make grants to such organizations as this, but I do think such an organization is worthy of a grant because it is doing a splendid job for the mining industry not only in British Columbia but in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
Interest in mining in British Columbia is general throughout the province, and is particularly apparent in the coastal region as the result of a recent supreme court decision. Development of new mining operations and increased production from existing operations can be anticipated, particularly with regard to crown-granted claims affected by that decision.
For years there has been a false idea that Vancouver island and the coastal area in general are areas where mineral deposits are small and uneconomic. This, of course, is not so. We have had several major producing mines on the coast. One of them is the mine at Britannia which has come to life again, and which I understand is rapidly expanding its production. The Granduc property near the head of Portland canal shows promise of being a major copper ore body, and there are a number of large ore bodies along the coast.
Shortly after I came down here I was in conversation with an official of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I pointed out to him the promising
5364	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys mineral potential of Vancouver island, particularly the northern area, and I referred to the desirability of encouraging the development of this potential under the roads to resources program. He disagreed with my view as to the resources there, and I asked him where he had got his information. He said he had got it from the department of mines. I think it is high time that the department of mines reassessed its estimate of the mineral potential of that area, because I think its assumptions are not based on sound or up to date information.
Just to show how wrong the department was, I am going to list some of the operating mines in the area as well as a number of known ore bodies awaiting development. On the southern end of Vancouver island we have Cowichan Copper, which was brought into production through the tenacity and perseverance of an old prospector and mining man in British Columbia named Ozzie McDonald. Great credit is due to him for bringing this mine into production, because many people had scorned its chance of ever becoming a success. Mount Washington Copper is another ore body which is being developed by the Noranda company, and it also has great possibilities. Further north, near Nimpkish lake, there is an important iron-producing property under development and large shipments are being made at the present time. There is also Quatsino Copper at Port McNeill, which is also concerned with the production of iron ore. There is a well known property near the northern end of the island called Coast Copper in which Consolidated Mining and Smelting holds a substantial interest. I believe they are anticipating a large expenditure there commencing almost immediately.
On the west coast there are innumerable mining properties. Many of the properties may not be very large, but with the network of roads that have been developed by the logging companies these mines could be economic producers and successful operations through the hooking up of these roads. The grouping of these ore deposits would provide a very substantial tonnage. We should benefit from the mistakes of the past and recall the experience in the United States. People did not think roads would be developed in that country. There were mines developed, one producing perhaps 500,000 tons in one area and another producing 500,000 tons in another area. In the old days these were considered uneconomic, but with the development of roads it was possible to take full advantage of such ore deposits. In many instances a very small mileage would be required to hook up existing roads and thus provide a very valuable transportation system.


I do not think the day is too far distant -indeed, I feel it is very close-when we are going to see once again a smelter on the coast particularly for the copper ores. In the Portland canal area a famous mine has come to life again. It is now called the Silbak-Premier; it used to be known as the old Premier mine. A tremendous amount of wealth was taken from this mine, which was later almost abandoned and thought to be worked out. I have an adventuresome brother who went in there last year, took a lease on the property and brought the property to life again. It has proved to be one of the outstanding mining rediscoveries in the country.
There is a great deal of activity in the development of iron ore, all of which is shipped to Japan. Ore shipments amount to approximately 1,000 tons a day from such mines as Texada Iron Mines, Silver Standard and others. Iron ore shipments are going from the west coast of the island, and substantial shipments will be going from the Queen Charlotte islands. By the end of this year the coastal area will be producing about
5,000	tons of iron ore per day. This, of course, is being exported to Japan. As well, there will be substantial shipments of copper and copper-nickel concentrates from coastal and interior mines.
While I can understand the British Columbia government's desire to conserve iron ore for ultimate processing in a long hoped-for steel mill, I think they have been seriously misguided in their efforts to promote the establishment of such a mill. They have discouraged the discovery and development of iron ore property. They now reserve for themselves in the coastal area 50 per cent of the iron content of any ore body, which pretty well eliminates any interest in prospecting in that area. The claims being developed and the properties being worked are largely the old crown grant claims. The difficulty to date in effecting the establishment of a steel mill on the coast has been the insufficient tonnage of known iron ore reserves.
I maintain that the only way they are going to increase these reserves is by giving more incentive to the prospecting and development of iron ore properties. I believe I can truthfully say that there is a much greater known reserve of iron ore on the coast of British Columbia than there was before a ton of it was shipped to Japan; because as these properties are developed-and most of them have been known for many years-they have found substantially greater ore reserves than the mining engineers and geologists anticipated. Mining legislation and taxation that discourages the prospecting for and proving

up of iron ore deposits will delay indefinitely the possibility of discovering the necessary tonnage. No one is going to waste time and money prospecting for new deposits of any minerals on the coast when the provincial government reserves to itself 50 per cent of the iron content of all ore.
My belief, and I think it is sound, is that investors in the highly speculative mining industry are entitled to every possible consideration in regard to taxation, depreciation allowances and government technical services. I know there exists in the minds of some a great fear that someone might make a little money out of a mine and not pay what they consider to be sufficient taxation. I would rather see an over-all development of mining even if we had to permit undue tax benefits to very large and successful operations, because if we are going to tax them the tax

ation seems to extend down to the little fellow and discourages the whole mining industry. It is my conviction that if neither government got a cent in direct taxation the employment in an active, healthy mining industry would pay dividends that would benefit the whole country.
In a large section of Vancouver island there is a situation that is a serious discouragement to the discovery and development of mines. About 1885 the provincial government of the day, in order to promote the construction of what is known as the E. & N. railway from Victoria to Courtenay on Vancouver island, made a grant including the lands, forests and minerals of one of the richest areas of the island. This grant went northward to the 50th parallel near Campbell River, and took in a strip approximately 20 miles wide extending from the south tip of the island.
At the time the grant was made my grandfather, who had then been settled in Comox valley for approximately 25 years, wrote a letter to his cousin in England stating as follows:
A railroad is being built between Victoria and Nanaimo-
At that time the terminus was intended to be Nanaimo. I continue:
-the company getting a strip of land about 20 miles back from the coast up as far as the Euclatawville.
For the information of hon. members who are not familiar with that part of the country the old Indian name applied to Seymour narrows was Euclatawville. I continue:
Did anyone ever hear of a more scandalous bargain? The M.P.P.'s should be strung up. Victoria and the neighbourhood is all those potheads care for.

I am sure there are many throughout the area who still feel the same about this as my grandfather did in those long-ago days. This grant ultimately passed into the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which still holds it, and their policies of administration are a serious handicap to mining development. They have no set royalty on mineral discoveries and deal with each deposit on a different basis. They not only want all that the traffic will bear in royalty but considerably more, and demand royalty on the gross- not on the net-returns to the investing mining company. Consequently companies are loath to make investments in an area where they run the risk of not only losing their own investment but of paying an exorbitant royalty to the Canadian Pacific Railway on the gross values produced.
On this score I do not think the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway are aware of the effect their policy is having in that area, because it would be to their own advantage in many other ways to have a healthy mining development in the E. & N. railway belt. I know myself of many properties that nobody will bother to stake, nobody will bother to spend any money on, simply because of the present policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I hope the minister will take this matter up immediately with the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway and endeavour to relieve this area of mineral development from the strangling policies of the company.
This so-called E. & N. belt is a perfect example of the dangers of giving large grants of resources to individual companies without any stipulation for their development. I hope the experience of 75 years will prove a useful lesson to all provincial governments, and to the federal government as well.

There are three points that I should like to put briefly before the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. In the first place, I should like to pay tribute to the splendid work which the hydrographic survey branch of his department has done in charting the coastal waters of my province.
As was pointed out earlier today, Newfoundland was discovered 463 years ago, and up to a year ago there was still part of our coastal waters not completely charted. The first charting of our waters was carried out by the British admiralty under the direction of the famous Captain Cook. With the few facilities that he had at his disposal at that time it is amazing how accurate his calculations were, but still it is essential that this work be pushed ahead, and we are grateful for the way in which the minister and this branch of his department are doing that job.

Two years ago, I think, there was some question as to who was in command of the survey ships when they were actually doing the survey work. There was some question whether the captain had actual command or whether the hydrographer had full command. I hope the minister will be able to tell us that this question has now been fully clarified so that no further confusion on this point can take place in the future.
The second point is one that I brought to the minister last year, and I am not going to repeat what I said then but simply draw to his attention the fact that as far as I have been able to find out nothing has been done with respect to the prevailing rate system of pay. I know the minister does not have full control over this, that it ties in with the Minister of Labour, and that there are other departments such as the Department of Transport, the Department of Fisheries and also the Department of National Revenue which have this problem. I would ask the minister to get together with his other colleagues on this matter and see whether something cannot be done about it, because I do not think it is good for morale to have men working side by side in a boat, or two little boats working side by side doing the same work exactly, yet with the men getting different rates of pay. As an employer I believe the federal government should follow the principle of equal pay for equal work.
The third point I wish to bring to the minister's attention has to do with the situation at the fluorspar mines at St. Lawrence. Last year it was discovered that those mines were subject to radiation hazards. I understood that some arrangement was to be worked out with the minister's department, or some mechanism would be installed, whereby the miners themselves would be able to monitor the amount of radiation so they would have a check against the monitoring done by the operators. I understood this was to be done by the miners themselves. Can the minister bring me up to date as to what progress has been made in that regard?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a word at this time with respect to two sections of the important Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. As others have done, I should like to congratulate the minister and in particular the divisional heads of the geological survey on the work they have carried out in the past year. I hope that what I say on this point will provide some encouragement to them to do more than they have done in the past.
Perhaps I might make reference, sir, to one important problem. A decision will have to be made eventually with respect to the


greatest known resource of oil in the world. I refer, of course, to the Athabasca tar sands. The committee is fully aware, of course, that a study has been made as to the feasibility of developing the tar sands by using a nuclear instrument. We are also familiar with the fact that the government of the province of Alberta, through the Alberta petroleum and natural gas conservation board, has undertaken and is continuing a study to determine other methods by which the sand can be separated from the oil and thus permit the crude oil to flow freely. I impress this on the minister, and perhaps he will comment on it.
We realize, of course, the international implications, and that it is quite obvious that we are not going to have a nuclear test until several other factors have been determined. First of all, of course, there is the disarmament conference which, among other things, involves the feasibility of banning any nuclear tests whatsoever. In my opinion this need not defer any studies or any work which should be undertaken eventually in the hope that when we resolve the international aspects of this problem we can then move ahead to determine how best we may be able to utilize this vast volume of oil.
I am not placing any particular urgency on it, because it is well known to the committee that in the province of Alberta we are already having some difficulty in marketing the oil we have at the present time. I do, nevertheless, impress on the minister and his department that we offer the utmost cooperation to the provincial officials and any persons in the industry who wish to undertake studies or research into either nuclear tests or any other separation process. We should make it abundantly clear in this committee that we shall do nothing to discourage the eventual development of those resources. I accept all the arguments on the importance of maintaining the health of our people, but having done this I suggest that we give every possible encouragement, as I have said, and I hope the minister will make some comment on what has happened thus far.
I would also hope that in the geological survey division the government will continue the practice of the last two years of putting as many young graduate geologists to work as they possibly can, because they will get no better experience anywhere in the field of geology. In addition, I know the minister recognizes that there are areas to which we have given perhaps too little attention, and what is perhaps even more important is that these young men could be very usefully employed in conducting investigations in these areas. I acknowledge the fact that the minister

has given some leadership in the past and has started a very active campaign in this respect, but I suggest that we could still improve on it by making use of added numbers of these people for the two reasons I have mentioned.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, 1 would ask the minister to examine the possibility of developing more research facilities than he now has in the department. He may shudder to think he would have to assume any further responsibilities in his department, but I feel that in relation to our resources we have not developed our research facilities to the fullest extent. For example, we should perhaps have a look at the possibility of using the byproducts of petroleum products as a rocket propellant. We might look at the possibility of upgrading various ores. There are a number of aspects that could be examined. I mention this because it would undoubtedly encourage further secondary industry and keep the basic product within Canada to a greater degree. It would follow, of course, that a greater number of Canadians would be employed if this should take place.
In this respect I have previously mentioned the problem of government in relation to resources. It does seem to me that the department now under consideration might take on some of the responsibilities which have been allocated to two other departments of government. If we look closely at the resources of Canada we find that jurisdiction with respect to them is roughly divided among three different departments of the government. In order to avoid the duplication that obviously must follow, and in order to centralize activity with respect to the promotion and development of our resources in so far as they are a federal responsibility, I suggest that the minister might take the lead in discussing with his colleagues the advantages of placing under his administration those responsibilities which are currently shared by two of his colleagues. Perhaps the most notable, of course, are those which come under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I am not suggesting that these same responsibilities might not come under the minister of that department, but I do think a centralization of the effort in this field in relation to all mineral products, not just petroleum products, under one department and one divisional head would be most beneficial.
May I conclude as I did in commencing my remarks by congratulating the minister and his officials on running what I consider, having had close association with it, a most efficient department, and I hope he will take these suggestions under advisement.

I was wondering whether the Chair would bear with me in this regard. There may be a chance that I will be absent on Monday, and I wanted to make a few


remarks in relation to this industry. I appreciate the fact that there is in the estimates a particular item so far as the coal board is concerned. If I may be permitted to do so, Mr. Chairman, I should like to continue.
Coming back, then, to the problem in Drumheller itself, may I say that there are approximately 600 men employed in the coal industry today in the Drumheller area, when it is operating. However, as I was saying, the soft coal is used only for domestic fuel, and the mines are in serious competition with natural gas and other fuels that have been competing with them in reference to this domestic market in the urban centres and the fuel now used by the farmers. The coal miners in that area, which is the area of Drumheller which takes in the towns of East Coulee, Wayne, Nacmine and others, work approximately only from December to March. The rest of the year they are unemployed and on unemployment insurance, or must seek employment in other fields of industry.
At the present time the problem is this, as many say. Why are these men not moved, or why do they not seek other types of employment? The situation, and it has been stated by other members in this house who represent coal mining areas, is briefly this. As to the coal miners themselves, all their investment is in their homes in these areas; and when they leave them they leave behind all their life savings. The situation is such that the coal employees themselves wish to remain in those areas even on short employment, because they do not want to give up their homes and their small savings.
I want to make myself doubly clear on two more points. One is that the coal mined in the Drumheller area is sub-bituminous coal, soft coal which is used as domestic fuel. There may be some opportunity for the use of this type of coal in reference to other products, but at the present time this area is depressed and employment in this area has been going down for the last four of five years. In fact ever since the war ended and their market for coal for use as fuel ended, there has been a considerable amount of unemployment in this area.
This reference may seem somewhat out of place, but we had the Springhill tragedy as a result of which certain steps were taken by the government. This is the point I want to make. I dealt with this problem in the budget debate and I want to be brief. Here we have an area with surplus labour because of the coal problem. Here we have an area with a plentiful water supply, with good agricultural land surrounding it. In fact in the Munson area we have some of the finest agricultural land in the world. It is the centre of the judicial districts in the province

of Alberta. It has good hard-top roads leading to the city of Drumheller from all leading cities, towns and villages, and Drumheller is situated on the main C.N.R. line.
It seems to me that when we have this surplus pool of labour as a result of the depressed coal mining industry, this would be an excellent site-and this is the point I am making-for the building of a penitentiary in the province of Alberta. We are the only province in the whole of Canada that does not have one of those federal institutions. In this way these people, numbering 500 or 600, or at least some of them would be able to find employment elsewhere than in the coal mines until some other industry develops in the area to use the coal and give them employment.
I therefore say today that I trust the minister, when this matter is considered by the government, will remember that this is one of the most depressed coal mining areas in the whole country; and when they are considering a federal institution for western Canada will decide that this is the spot at which it should be built.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words on this particular item of the department. As the committee probably knows, 1 represent one of the large mining communities in the pre-Cambrian shield, and I am very interested in the mines department. However, as a miner who worked in the mines in the pre-Cambrian shield for many years, I never at any time saw any mines officials from the federal government; I never came into contact at any time with agents of the federal government or of the department of mines, and as far as I know none of my colleagues in the mines had ever done so.
So we begin to wonder just what the department is for, who it works for and what is the purpose of the department. I notice that a number of officials are present in the gallery. Each of them must head a separate branch, and I would be interested to know how many of them are connected with the part of the department which is concerned with mines.
We want to be fair, and I must congratulate the department on the valuable work which has been done for Canada on a national scale in the field of mapping and surveys. I have talked to many United States pilots and others who have used maps prepared by the department, and they claim that these maps are better than any maps which are available from any other source. As I say, I think the department is to be congratulated on the high calibre of the work which has been done in this particular department. The fact that Canada has, in the main, been mapped, means that we can assess the possibilities and be in a position to make the best use of them. Certainly the work which has been done, particularly in those areas where few or no people live and which have, in the main, been entered only by survey teams, is of a high calibre.
However, as to the other half of the department, that which deals with mines, I think less can be said in favour of its activities. I have here a booklet which is put out by the department under the name of the director of the mines branch setting out the history of the branch and describing the work it does. The booklet is certainly comprehensive and the branch has a great deal of equipment and machinery, by the look of it. I do know that the branch has done some useful work for particular companies with regard to the processing of ores and other things of that nature, but I suggest that this work might

Mr. Chairman, before the
luncheon adjournment I was outlining the fact that there are problems created by the division of responsibility for mineral resources between the provincial and federal governments. There should be more co-operation between the two bodies and more authority in this field should be assumed by the federal government. An assessment should be made of the full potentiality of our mineral resources. I cite what has been done by the national energy board as an example. An assessment of this kind would assist the development of our resources on a national rather than a provincial scale.
Many known ore deposits are not being developed now because of conditions existing in the provinces. In my own province we are interested in the development at Steep Rock where an open pit and deep mine operation have been undertaken. We are interested in taking full advantage of those natural resources. We are also interested in the development at the Belcher islands, at Kirkland lake and at Kapuskasing where there are known iron reserves which have not been developed.
The method of financing mining companies has created a problem concerning the overall mineral distribution in Canada. Mines in the Belcher islands could be developed advantageously. Problems would have to be overcome but the opening up of the north would be greatly assisted. Assistance should be given to the companies in the Belcher islands. This would mean a deep seaport being established at Moosonee and an extension of a railway into the area. New development would take place with international implications. We would likely have to export to markets other than United States markets. The people of northern Ontario feel it would be advantageous to develop some of our mineral resources for new markets

in Europe in addition to United States markets. They feel we should not place our eggs in one basket. A large United States company holds mining rights at Dane. The company has no intention of developing the property but proposes to keep it as a future potential source as it keeps other property it holds throughout the world.
The federal Department of Mines and Technical Surveys should eventually develop a liaison with the provinces under which there would be recognized the right of the federal government to ascertain the value to Canadians of the development of our national resources.
All hon. members are familiar with the uranium problem. Operations in this field should have been restricted. The government should have assessed the potential reserves of uranium and the anticipated markets. The department should have had some concept of the potentiality of reserves in relation to the demand on the world markets. If the department did have this knowledge the development of uranium at Bancroft and particularly at Elliot Lake should have been curtailed. We have spent more money in the development of Elliot Lake than we will ever get back out of it unless the present circumstances radically alter.
If mines are to be assisted under federal legislation, as one hon. member suggested they should be, we should determine what we want to have accomplished in this field. We made a mistake in enacting legislation that made possible the financing of an uranium development that had only a limited life time and limited sales. The mines could not possibly have made the money they did without taking advantage of the situation on the scale they did. It is rumoured that one financier borrowed up to $40 million in the United States to establish a mining operation at Elliot Lake. Through subsidies and the sale of the contract he had-it was a government affair-he paid back the money, took $10 million and entered the exploitation field. He is now working in the Arctic region in the development of an oil industry.
I suggest that these people are taking advantage of the federal government. They are taking advantage of the very things that were made available to them to allow the mines to be developed. They are now using this privilege and, in many cases, abusing it, because we were shortsighted in allowing the condition to develop. The minister may say that this does not come within his jurisdiction and it is not his field, and he may be right because, as I said before, I am not too sure what are the rights and privileges of the mines branch.

The advantages that the mining companies get flow from the federal government and therefore in my opinion the federal department must take some responsibility in this matter. I believe that in fields such as gold mining, where we give emergency assistance, the mines department should take an interest in the industry. I have made the point, and certainly other hon. members have made it also, that the inspection of the mines toward which we are paying assistance is nil, especially when the amount of money paid over is taken into consideration. We are not in agreement that all those companies are honest, for the simple reason that, as an example, one of the mining companies in northern Ontario for years bragged about having a portfolio of $70 million. They have now taken this portfolio and have gone into the steel industry and into a number of other interests. They have taken that money out of the community and the country and it is no longer available even for pensions for their employees or for retiring some of the debt of the communities that had to be built to allow the company to make the money it originally put into its portfolio.
We think the department has some responsibility in such fields as safety. I do not think it should go into it in the same way as the provincial governments do, but a great deal of work must be done in the field of silicosis. It is not enough to say that silica dust in the lungs is a very bad thing and then pour into the same lungs a great deal of aluminum dust and say it will solve the problem. When we do that we have covered up the problem but we have not solved it. The responsibility for this type of research should not rest entirely with the provinces because each province has adopted a different attitude, and the problem is not the same in the mining industry in all provinces.
The federal government has an exceedingly important role to play in this field in the Northwest Territories where it has done very little for the protection of its miners. Many of the miners coming back to the fields in which I have worked have been in very poor physical condition. They have suffered and have been able to get very little recompense for their suffering. I attended a meeting in Elliot Lake not too long ago where the problem of radiation was under discussion. It is very interesting to know that no regulations have been drawn up in this regard. While this may be a provincial matter, the federal government must assume some responsibility because we are responsible for that industry being born in the first place in that area. We control their sales. We loaned them the money; we gave them the tax exemptions which made it possible for
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys them to be there, so we have some responsibility. Yet, some of the mines have not even granted their employees the right to obtain a urinalysis to determine radiation effects. We have supplied no film strips, no matter what the jobs are.
I was very surprised to know that to such men as repairmen and men working in high concentrations of uranium production, some of the mines give urinalysis tests which determine the radiation effects. Others do not bother doing so. They have pointed out that there was no reason why they should do so.
These are fields in which the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys can serve a useful function for all the Canadian people, and particularly the people who work in that industry and their families. They must exercise some responsibility in this field. I would suggest in particular that in these fields in which the federal government makes a large contribution it should assume much more authority and much more responsibility with respect to industrial relations and safety measures than it does now. I see no reason why the government cannot do that.
For years I have been interested in learning why the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys explosives division did not do something about demanding a change in the type of explosives used in mines. Many of the employees suffer more from exposure from nitrogen gases than they do from exposure to dust. Many miners will tell you that this nitrogen gas, by burning the linings and the membranes of the nose, throat and lungs, eliminates the hairs and other protection which were there originally and that a great deal of the problem that develops, along with silicosis, is brought about by nitrogen in the gases caused by the explosion of ordinary nitrogen.
There are other types of explosives which could be used which have no large amounts of nitrogen in them and which would serve the same purpose. They would probably cost a little more money but in relation to the amount of material that could be produced in a mine, which is attached to this problem, the cost factor probably would be greatly reduced because of the increased efficiency and increased production that would take place by a simple change in the type of explosives used in the mine.
Then there is the matter of government subsidies and government assistance in the mining field. As I pointed out, in my opinion this gives the federal government a great deal more authority than it has ever exercised in this industry. We have the problem of coal in British Columbia and in the maritimes. In
5374	HOUSE OF
Supply*-Mines and Technical Surveys those areas the production of coal has been greatly reduced. At the same time we are paying very high subventions on coal from the maritimes. We have tried to solve these problems in one way but we have not really solved anything at all. We have accomplished very little except to postpone the time when the inevitable will take place. This is true with respect to emergency gold mining assistance. We have never opposed the assistance because it was absolutely necessary when it was put into effect to alleviate a problem over which neither the mines, the employees nor the mining communities have any control. But this type of subsidy has been used for the protection only of the industry and the few results which will flow from that protection, such as a given number of jobs and a slight wage increase.
The wage increases flowing from this assistance have been very slight. The wage increases which have taken place have flowed, in my opinion, more from automation in the mines than anything else. A large mine that used to have 3,000 employees is now operating and turning out the same tonnage with from 900 to 1,200 employees. Obviously production per man has increased to such an extent that they could easily double the wages without adding to the cost factor. Very little of the benefit that the mines sometimes claim flow from the emergency gold mining assistance returns to the community in the form of wages and spending by the employees of that industry.
I am sure that this problem is common in the coal industry. This is why I am afraid it is going to exist in Elliot Lake. I would not be the least bit surprised to find the department suggesting to the minister that we should stock-pile uranium; that the government should buy it and should make some attempt to keep those mines operating on a partial basis. I would rather see Elliot Lake close down tomorrow than have this happen, than have them carry on for the next 15 or 20 years on a subsistence level where they are not able to increase wages and living standards. I do not want to see them remain in the kind of situation that has existed in the maritimes for years and in my own area where gold is the principal product. I would much rather see these mines closed down completely and the municipalities have to fend for themselves and find secondary industries. If the minister looks at the problem at all I think his conclusion will be similar to mine. If assistance by way of subsidy, subvention or otherwise from the federal government is going to go into these areas, let us at least make it in a form that the areas can develop and help themselves.


While this type of hand-out has served a purpose and will serve a purpose, in my opinion it is only justifiable if it is carried on for a short period of time until other assistance of a permanent nature can be provided. As far as I am concerned, some of the assistance under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act should have been earmarked for secondary industries and secondary development in the mining fields. It should not have been left wholly to the mines to do what they felt like doing about it because in many cases it has been of very little benefit to the areas concerned.
In many cases, however, the mines have done an admirable job and in my area there is one that in my opinion has been well managed. I never liked the manager. I have negotiated with him and we never saw eye to eye. I have known him for a long time and he is a rough, tough fellow who knows what mining is all about. I refer to Mr. Ken Gray who is the manager of Sylvanite mine and also controls it to a large extent. He is a man who in my opinion has practised all possible conservation methods and has taken full advantage of assistance under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. But in reading the Northern Miner I find that even with this type of leadership the mine is going to close down. This is inevitable because emergency gold mining assistance will only help them up to a point. This community is going to be faced not with an emergency gold mining problem but with an emergency problem involving the community itself in which gold will not be a factor because unless the price of gold increases considerably we are not going to be able to do the prospecting and development necessary to bring in very low grade properties.
I hope the government does not follow the course that it appears they might follow. I say "appears" in the light of the reports made from time to time by the committee originally established to consider the problem of Elliot Lake. In my view Elliot Lake is a specific problem that can be solved in a specific way because it only has to do with uranium mines, but on one occasion the house leader got up and dragged in Bancroft and Uranium City and said he would not be able to do anything for Elliot Lake that he could not do for Bancroft and Uranium City. The problem is not the same at all.
The mines at Bancroft and Uranium City have been operating for quite a number of years. There are also other interests in these areas. When you throw in a number of unrelated problems you confuse the issue. The issue is no longer clear-cut. The problem

can be solved quite easily by paying a subsidy or subvention or doing something else to enable the industry to carry on at a limited capacity and with a very low rate of production. It seems to me this is going to be the solution, and I should like to caution the minister about using a subvention of this type to help to solve the problem of the uranium industry. The problem in the Elliot Lake area can be solved by putting money into bringing in secondary industries and conserving the mines for the day when they can be operated at peak efficiency. The day will come when uranium may be used in steel production and other things. In the meantime I hope that the minister does not confuse the problem with all the other problems that can be and have been introduced in the past in this field.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to speak except on the technical surveys branch of the department but having listened to the hon. member for Timis-kaming who has just taken his seat I feel I must comment on and disagree with one statement he made. I may not have heard him correctly but I understood him to say that when some of these mines, and he mentioned a number of them, get into difficulties they should close down completely rather than struggle along. I cannot agree with that at all. If this were carried to its logical conclusion it would mean the closing down of a good many of the coal mines in the maritimes which have struggled along and a good many other mines which have struggled along and provided a minimum subsistence for a number of people, thus enabling them to remain in their home towns. The hon. member made a very broad statement and as a broad statement I think it was incorrect. In my view there are a good many occasions when people are justified in continuing to carry on as best they can in the hope that some change will come for the better.
I should like to speak for a minute or two about the question of technical surveys. This department has a major role to play in the development of Canada. Unlike some of the other departments of government, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has to take the lead rather than follow. In the case of many departments they cannot operate until the country is opened up and proper conditions prevail. The reverse is true of this department. Those who work for it must go into unmapped and uncharted territory, make surveys and maps and locate resources before other departments can follow in their path.
24, 1960	5375
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
To keep this lead we need a large supply of able and enthusiastic scientific personnel. As the department is now constituted it has a very satisfactory nucleus of specialists in the highly specialized fields which we find throughout the department. But when the mines, forests and waters committee examined the estimates of this department last year the members of the committee discovered that one of the greatest difficulties concerned the retention of scientific personnel in Canada, people with the ability to carry out geological surveys, mapping and other work in our northern territories. It was found that these people were easily attracted elsewhere by the great differential in salaries.
At one time it was considered that the government service was one of the better services in which to work but gradually this changed to the point where, up until quite recently, the government service was declining. Industry became the most lucrative field of endeavour and until recently the universities were in second place because they had raised their standards. The branches of the government were gradually declining. I was very pleased to see that the latest salary increases proposed will include improved salaries for scientific personnel and will cover a great many of the people now in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys whom this country needs very badly.
We also need to bring into the country and educate here other persons who have special scientific abilities for the jobs that they will undertake. I was pleased to learn in the research committee recently that the salaries and working conditions of scientific personnel are improving. The president of the national research council, who is very much concerned with the standards of scientists in this country, many of whom eventually find their way into the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, stated that there is now a net immigration into Canada of scholars seeking postdoctorate fellowships.
In other words, the Canadian reputation for scientific advance and research is increasing throughout the world and more people are coming to this country to receive advanced scientific education in research than are going from this country to receive such education elsewhere. As a result of the high standard that is being set in Canada, I feel we are becoming well recognized in the scientific field.
I was also pleased to hear the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration recently invite persons from the United States particularly to come to Canada in order to help to develop this country. A few years ago this suggestion
5376	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys might have been considered fantastic. For many years the flow was the other way. I think it is not such a fantastic thing now. We are hopeful that persons who come here to receive advanced scientific training will be more inclined to stay; and I think that many may take seriously the request of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to come to this country and to help to develop it.
There is one other matter I should like to mention in connection with this department. This concerns our advance in the field of radio-astronomy. On June 20 the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys opened at Penticton, British Columbia the new radio astrophysical observatory. This observatory brings Canada into the field of radio-astronomy for the first time. The radio telescope at White lake near Penticton is not the largest in the world. That honour is reserved for the radio telescope at Jodrell Bank in England. However, it is a radio telescope on a scale comparable to that of others established in North America and in various other parts of the world and it will assist our astronomers and those persons interested in space research to obtain information which it is absolutely impossible to obtain by observation, even with the best telescope that is available. These things indicate that Canada is advancing in the scientific field and that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is keeping up with the most recent advances in astronomy and in the other scientific endeavours which it has undertaken for the development of this country.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
I am one of two members of the House of Commons who represent one of the most famous mining areas in Canada, namely the Kootenay mining area in the southeastern portion of British Columbia. I had the pleasure and the opportunity as a young man to know a good many of the early pioneer men in the mining industry, and some of the pioneer women, who helped to build up the mining industry in the interior, including the at that time well known Nels Demers who went into the Kootenays in 1856 and stayed there until 1910.
When I look over at the genial minister who has charge of this socialist type of service to society I find it extremely difficult to be critical, and I will not be very critical this afternoon. I simply want to make a few suggestions and a few observations as a result of my contact with the department on various occasions and my experience around the country in the various mining companies in my constituency and meeting persons interested in mining and others.

This department which carries on essential services in research, scientific work and technical work that is essential in the location, surveying and the proper and adequate development of our natural resources is somewhat generally considered to be a non-contentious and non-political department, a department that does not arouse much contention or controversy. However, it contains a staff which is performing an essential and, to many people, little known service to this country. I say that because I have had the opportunity to* discuss the work of this department with various groups, when I have been speaking to groups in the constituency and in other places.
I am amazed at how little is known by the average Canadian outside of the mining industry and the universities, of the essential work that is undertaken by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and' that so little is known as to the valuable information that can be obtained from this department, its reports, its publications, its officials and its staff. While this information is essential and valuable to the mining industry and to others interested in the development of other natural resources, I think much greater use could be made of this information on a wider scale on the part of people who are interested in the development of this country.
Interest in this department has been stimulated in recent years in my constituency and in the Kootenay area generally because of its officials and staff taking some part in the surveys in the Columbia river basin. That work has brought the people of the district for the first time, in many cases, in contact with the engineers and the other staff conducting these surveys. As a result of that contact I notice an increased interest in the work of the department and, as a result, inquiries as to where they can obtain maps, information and so on.
I want to make a suggestion or two. I suggest these parties are working for the people of Canada, not for any particular group. Their work is usually directly related to some development. When a party goes into an area the people of the area are obliged to depend on casual information and, in some cases, on rumour. I think there should be a form of press release issued periodically so that the people will know what this survey crew is doing as part of a larger project and so on. It is only right and I think it would be well for the department. I think that would be interesting information and very much worth-while information. I have had that suggestion made to me by a number of people in my constituency who are greatly interested in the work of the department.

In addition to that, I think it is ministers who usually give talks to public meetings and various organizations. I am quite sure that the officials and members of the staff in any given locality would foe quite willing to co-operate with local organizations, for instance, as was done in the Columbia river basin where there were parties of this department in that basin for years. I think it would be an excellent idea if the appropriate engineer or person would give a chat to the Rotary club or to the chamber of commerce in this area on the particular work of the department and the project that is being undertaken and the scientific information it is trying to obtain.
In this connection I want to quote very briefly from page 31 of the report. I have read a considerable part of this report before but not all of it. It says:
The Vancouver office gave information and assistance to industrialists and others interested in metallic and industrial minerals, engineering geology, ground-water supplies, and construction materials. A number of short term field projects were carried out by the staff geologists, mainly at the request of other government departments among which were engineering-geology reports on dam and power sites along the Columbia river. Activity at the office continued to increase: there were more than 8,039 visitors, and 17,705 copies of publications of various kinds were distributed.
This is all to the good but the information is going largely to persons directly interested in the mining industry or to governments or persons interested in the development of hydro power, and things of that sort. I suggest that having this extra organization with the information as well as the Vancouver office it could be used to greater advantage by making certain the information was available to high schools and other various organizations through appropriate outlets.
I think something more should be done to let the people know what information can be obtained, the maps which are available and the services which are available through this department. I know the larger corporations know all about it. Officials of Consolidated Miming and Smelting Corporation told me that they have had wonderful contacts with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. They get every co-operation and other companies do as well. But I suggest that this department should also make certain it does all it can to serve all the people, such as the smaller mining companies -I have run into cases where they were not aware of the services rendered by this department-prospectors and others.
I should like the minister when he replies to indicate what arrangements are made with provincial departments of mines or other related departments to avoid any overlapping
24, 1960	5377
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys in services or expenditures. I realize when speaking on this question that natural resources generally speaking come within the jurisdiction of provincial governments; but I would like the minister to inform the committee what is done in the way of consultation with provincial departments of mines and related branches of government to make sure there is no overlapping in any work being undertaken in surveys and things like that, or in publications, thereby creating unnecessary expenditure.

speechtext:
Following on the lines of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni when he spoke this morning, I want to bring to the minister's attention the excellent work which has been done over the course of 50 years by the interior chamber of mines which has its headquarters at Nelson, British Columbia. That organization is financed by subscriptions from local mining companies interested in smelting, mining and so on. I want to ask the minister if he would inform the committee if co-operation exists between his department and organizations such as chambers of mines in the development of knowledge of the work undertaken by the department.
I suggest that as most of these chambers of mines-and in British Columbia there is the chamber of mines in Vancouver and in the interior we have the interior chamber of mines in Nelson-are located on a main or well travelled street, usually with good window space. They could be used as an agency or a medium to advertise the work of this department and the information which is available in the form of publications, maps, and so on. I think they would be very willing to co-operate in this respect. Nelson is the centre for the Kootenay West area and people going there could get this information.
There is an increasing interest amongst these people in where they can obtain maps of the Columbia river basin area. The department has published some excellent maps in that respect and I think I have copies of maps covering the whole basin. But I get frequent inquiries and I think this would be a valuable outlet for information. I am sure the interior chamber of mines would be only too willing to co-operate. They could also provide information as to the services offered with respect to checking up on certain ores, recommending certain processes and treatments and so on.
I have another suggestion. I am one inclined to travel around the hills and mountains and I have been interested in the geological surveys which have been undertaken all through the southeastern interior. This is
5378	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys very necessary work when it comes to the consideration of hydro development and I have one suggestion to make. I notice that the longer I talk the sadder the minister looks. I suggest that instead of having just a number on a given monument, which is usually just a cement post and a copper or bronze plug in the top of it, it would be much more interesting to local people, travellers or tourists to have the elevation mentioned at the same time. Usually there is a number on the post, like "No. 96 geological survey", and if you want any information you write for it. I think with very little extra expense you could have the elevation marked on the plug and on the monument as well which would make for much more interest. I advance that as a suggestion.
The final matter on my list of very mild complaints is this. The minister knows I am interested in this because a good number of my constituents are interested as well as visitors from the south who come up by water craft along the Columbia lakes up as far north as Revelstoke. They are interested in obtaining a chart to assist them in navigation. The minister knows about this because last year he informed me that his department was very busy and had not had time to work on charts of this sort. I suggested that they could be sold at a price which would show little expense to the treasury. I am sure that everybody using water craft would be willing to pay a dollar in order to be able to find a safe channel from the international boundary to the south up as far as Revelstoke. When the minister replies I would like him to tell me what progress is being made in the preparation of a chart suitable for navigation purposes from the international boundary along the Columbia as far north as Revelstoke.
I have a few more remarks to make on appropriate items, but at this point I shall resume my seat.

speechtext:
I would like to reply to something said by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka when he attributed to me the suggestion that many small mines would close down. I worked for 15 years in a small mine and I would be the last one to suggest that we do anything which would close the mines down; but we do suggest that the end result will produce the position which I am sure is in the minds of the people who suggested that aid should be given.
Looking at it in retrospect I am sure we could solve the problem of the few communities who depend on this industry. I am sure we could take a few million dollars and resolve some of the problems in the same way as we solved the subsidy question
[Mr. Herridge.l
in relation to coal. All I say is that we have tried this method and it has not been satisfactory as far as the communities were concerned. There have continued to be emergency problems, and I suggest this step should be taken not in the uranium industry but that assistance be given to those communities for which we are responsible. Our responsibility to them is not necessarily to keep the mines in operation just for the sake of operating them; it is a responsibility to the people of the community to see that some alternative is provided for the employment of those working in mines which may cease to operate.
May I say I am surprised that the department of mines is not making greater effort to assist the coal mines industry in the maritimes. I am surprised that the government has not undertaken a research program in that area perhaps with a view to producing a form of distillation such as is used in Germany. I understand that when a deep coal mine has been shut down one can close everything off, drill holes into it and begin burning the coal in seams where the coal is not of an economic grade. A methane gas is thus produced which, while it may not be suitable for burning in homes, can be used in the manufacture of steel and other industrial purposes. This particular suggestion may be of no great value, but it seems to me some solution must be found to the problems of these people in the maritimes who have long been dependant upon this industry.
We should not wait until a problem develops before action is taken. Before we develop a new industry, such as the uranium industry, let us in future decide what the industry is worth to the Canadian people and the purpose it is intended to serve. Then let us go all out to get the most out of it for the benefit of Canadians and the economy generally. All too often the action taken is haphazard and uncontrolled. For example, we are still drilling hundreds and hundreds of oil wells every year, yet the hon. member for Calgary South tells us that there is a great problem about selling the gas which we are already producing. This seems to me rather silly. What is needed is for the department of mines to make an estimate of our potential and an estimate of what our needs are going to be. Then we could develop this natural resource so that the Canadian people can get the most benefit out of the industry.

I agree entirely with what the hon. member says. That is exactly what I was trying to say. These things should be a matter of common sense. We know that the Borden report gave us a lot of information as to the needs of the Canadian people and the productive capacity available. What I am saying is that the department of mines has not asserted its right to decide what is going to be done about it.
The natural resources of Canada belong to the people as a whole yet we are continuing to drill for oil, although we already have more than we can sell. Not only that, but I understand we are going to buy oil from Russia and other places. I think the department of mines should be in a position to govern these things and do something about what is contained in the Borden report.
This brings up another question which puzzles me. I read all the reports which are presented to the house and perhaps I did the department a disservice in my opening remarks by not referring to all the publications which have been put out. I did not mean to imply that the department is not doing any
24, 1960	5379
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys work in this regard. All I was trying to say was that they were not doing their work in the mining field in the way in which I should like to see it done. Reports such as the Borden commission report are placed before the government and before the Canadian people. Politicians tear them apart and say they are good reports, or that they are not good reports, but what does the government do about it? What good are these reports if no action follows as a result? In the short period during which I have been here I have seen very little effort on the part of the government to implement the recommendations made by these commissions.
I should like to say a few words now about the assistance which is provided to the gold mining industry and subsidies to industry in general. The gold mining assistance act was introduced, first of all, as an emergency measure but it has continued until the present time and the word "emergency" has not yet been taken out of the title. Today the industry is facing the same problem as it was facing in 1948 and the government has given no indication that it intends to consider some form of long term solution in which the gold mining industry would be interested.
One of the most satisfactory solutions would, of course, be the raising of the price of gold to the producers. If the present method of assistance were used in order to assist other industries, that is, emergency measures rather than long term solutions, I do not think the consequences would be at all favourable and while we do not want to put any company out of business, it would seem desirable that the government should consider some other method of assisting communities dependent on the mining industry. We would be well advised to try another method of helping the industry along the lines of a long term solution which would not be in the nature of an emergency measure.
