speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first I should like to thank the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) for his complimentary remarks directed at the officials and other employees of my department. His compliments were so sincere that they even elicited a discreet warning from the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier).
In reply to the request of the hon. member for Villeneuve, I intend next year to prepare, for the benefit of all hon. members, a report on the activities of my department in the previous year, and also a brief outline of the program for the current year, with particular regard to geological, topographical, geographical and other assignments. Such information will be useful to every hon.
5380	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys member when the estimates of my department are taken up in the house.
(Text):
The hon. members for Villeneuve, Port Arthur and the Yukon have referred to the recommendation of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters concerning the indicated need for expansion of the activities of my department. I should like to assure them that I have studied these recommendations with my officials and we have attempted to plan what we believe is the needed expansion of departmental activities for the next five years. This plan will be reflected in our future estimates to the limit that it can be accommodated in the future budgets of our government.
(Translation):
The hon. member for Villeneuve has raised a number of questions, such as federal aid to Quebec roads, the mining exploration program carried out by the Eldorado Mining and Refining Company and finally the transfer to the provinces of the resources found in the continental shelf. Such matters are not the responsibility of my department, but I shall be pleased to discuss them with those of my colleagues who are concerned.
(Text):
Recommendations were also made by the hon. members for Villeneuve and Port Arthur to the effect that we should increase the number of university students we employ in the summer months. There is a limit to the number of students we can accommodate without decreasing the efficiency or accuracy of our work. In years when work opportunity makes possible the employment of only a limited number of students we are always willing to take on more of them provided we know soon enough in advance to properly plan for larger size or additional field parties. I should like to mention that of the 786 geology students in our universities this year my department provided jobs for 245 of them; that is, 32 per cent or nearly one third of the total number of students.
I was pleased to hear the comments of the hon. member for Port Arthur concerning the economic reports of our mineral resources division such as those on iron ore. I can assure the hon. gentleman that more of this type of report are contemplated.
The hon. member for Port Arthur also asked what my department is doing in the form of research which could lead to more uses for uranium. May I say that in 1959, following discussions with Eldorado Mining and Refining, a research project was initiated by our mines branch for the development of non-nuclear uses for uranium. Eldorado made a grant of $10,000 to cover the salary of one engineer and incidental expenses relating to
[Mr. Comtois.l

the project. Prior to the arrival of the Eldorado engineer on November 1, 1959 some experimental alloying work had already been undertaken in the ferrous and non-ferrous fields. Attention was focussed on possible modifications of various types of steels when these are used in large tonnages. Aluminum, copper, magnesium and some other metals were also investigated. The basis of the research was related to the affinity that uranium has to oxygen, nitrogen, carbon, sulphur and other elements. At the present time there are four engineers and three technicians who are employees of the mines branch engaged in this work. The staff provided by Eldorado Mining and Refining consists of one engineer and two technicians. However, they have increased their original grant to $100,000. This increase was made to provide funds for an additional staff of four engineers and five technicians.
Investigations have indicated that small amounts of uranium might have very important results in improving the physical properties of steels used for many purposes. A few examples which may be quoted are axles, shafting, chain, high temperature tubing, piping, bolts and tool steels. Rolling tests have been carried out at a Canadian steel plant which proved that the uranium bearing steels are not difficult to work. In fact they reacted similarly to ordinary carbon steels in the rolling process. Steels are being made up at the present time in order to actually fabricate items which will be tried in service.
If the service tests duplicate the experimental results already obtained in the laboratory the whole program will be pushed forward another important step. It should be pointed out, however, that large steel tests will eventually have to be carried out before any item may be considered successful. There are variations in every stage of the process as one scales up such a laboratory test. It is anticipated that should one use prove successful, there will be more and more uses discovered over a period of time, which will pyramid the use of uranium in the metals industry.
May I also say that steps are far advanced for the creation of a research foundation which would help finance research in new uses of uranium. This project has been initiated by the uranium mining industry. Eldorado Mining and Refining Company of Canada and the mines branch of my department would most likely be associated with the foundation, making it a joint industry-government venture.
The hon. member for Port Arthur has asked how information was gathered in connection with a turndown of a request for

a road to a mining property in his constituency. Most of the information was obtained from the president of the company when he appeared before the interdepartmental roads appraisal committee and in subsequent discussions with officers of my department. The conclusion reached by my officers as a result was that considerable additional work had to be done before the prospect could be considered an economic proposition, and hence at this stage federal participation in a road to the property would be inadvisable.
I should also like to assure the hon. member that this government is very alert to the question of the further processing of ores and minerals in Canada including the possible use of direct reduction processes in the case of iron ores. A cabinet committee exists of which I am a member. This committee constantly keeps the situation under review and stands ready to encourage by any reasonable means the further processing of ores and minerals in our country.

speechtext:
I think it is the best possible one under the circumstances, and we will avoid any disagreements at some later date. This is a natural demarcation line, one that should always be very simple to maintain. It
24, 1960	538I
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys is a line that requires no markings. The markings are already in place, everything is ready, and I hope that before long we shall have succeeded in finding a final answer to this problem.
Mr. Chairman, I was also asked a question by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate (Mr. Pickersgill). This being the first time he deals with the problem, I think the hon. member for Laurier might enlighten him on the matter, which so far has always been considered as coming exclusively within the purview of the two provinces concerned.
Again I repeat that if we intervene in this matter, it will only be as go-betweens, to help reach a settlement. I assume that the authorities of the provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec, who are on very friendly terms, will be unable to refuse each other anything. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate should have no difficulty in persuading his Quebec friends.
As far as my department is concerned, we shall always be happy to offer the services of our team to establish the boundary line once and for all. I doubt, however, that the problem can be settled before some time, because in this case it is not a boundary such as the one between Ontario and Quebec, and I am not sure whether the premiers of the two provinces will be able to reach agreement. I hope so, but in any event it will be the responsibility of the premiers of those two provinces to settle the matter, and I repeat that our attitude towards the problem will always remain the same.
(Text):
In reply to a question by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, I wish to inform him that as far as the safety of the ships and personnel is concerned the responsibility rests fully with the sailing master of the ships, and definite instructions have been issued to that effect.
As far as wages of ships' crews are concerned, I had taken note of the problem because the hon. member had spoken to me about it. I can tell him that the same day that we spoke about the matter I got in touch with the Minister of Labour and he agreed that this problem had to be settled. He admitted it seemed unfair and that it should be settled and I have a memorandum prepared for him explaining the situation and 1 am quite sure it will be settled once and for all.
With respect to the St. Lawrence fluorspar mine, may I inform the hon. member that requests have been received by our mines
5382	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
branch for assistance toward monitoring radiation. The matter is being discussed with the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The hon. member for Pictou asked a question about the berthing of departmental ships in Pictou. I can assure him that we are planning to berth some of our ships at Pictou next winter, namely the same ones as least year. I think this answers his question.
In reply to the hon. member for Calgary South, I can only inform him that the technical feasibility committee has not yet handed in its report. Research and investigations are still being conducted in our mines branch, and by Richfield Oil Company.
The hon. member for Kootenay West asked what is being done to avoid the duplication of work with the provinces. Our directors of branches-geology survey and so forth- meet every year with officials of the provinces and discuss programs and projects to avoid duplication and to learn of the priority needs of the provinces in certain surveys which we then undertake. Our association with the chambers of mines is on a very friendly basis. We supply them with copies of our maps and reports and generally support any of their activities which have something in common with my department.
We have not yet got around to producing a chart of the Columbia river from the United States border to Revelstoke. We plan to undertake this as soon as possible. I can assure the hon. member for Kootenay West that I will do my best to see that the work is done and that we can produce the chart. I do not know how many copies can be sold. The hon. member mentioned $1 a copy, but how many copies could be sold at that price? That is what I do not know. This chart will cost a great deal of money. I do not expect we could ever be reimbursed by the sales made. Anyway I shall certainly discuss this matter with my officials and will do my best to satisfy the hon. member for the benefit of his wonderful district. I can say that.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: I thank the minister for the statement. Possibly I was a bit optimistic, but I would say that at the present time there would be anywhere from 100 to 200 conies sold a year. About 100 boats came up from the United States last year.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
They might buy more than one at a time and give some to their friends.
There is another matter that I wish to clear up. The hon. member for Laurier brought up again this matter of helicopters. To begin with, I should like to say something about Okanagan Helicopters Limited.

In my statement in the house on April 13, in answer to the charges made by the hon. member for Laurier respecting Autair Helicopter Services Limited, it was my concern to be as fair as possible to all parties involved. However, after reading over my statement, particularly the part which contains a passing reference to the sources of the hon. member's information, I wish to correct any wrong impression this statement may have left quite unintentionally. I wish to make it clear that it was not my purpose to imply that Okanagan Helicopter Services Limited had directed the hon. member for Laurier to raise the matter in the house, nor did I want to imply that the hon. gentleman had obtained all of his information from officials of the company.
I wish to assure the house that the high standards of operations of Okanagan Helicopter Services Limited have always been recognized by myself and officials of my department, and that the recent discussion with respect to this year's helicopter operations, in support of our polar continental shelf expedition, has not altered the high esteem which we have for this company. I want to make that statement to be fair to the company.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: Would the minister allow me to interrupt? I thank him for having made that statement but I should like to say that I have never on any occasion spoken to any of the officers of Okanagan Helicopter in connection with this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
Thank you. I wish to correct the impression I may have given to the house. There are some details I should like to clear up to the best of my knowledge and ability. With respect to the matter of a letter of intent, the hon. member for Laurier will recall that there was mention made of such a letter by him. In answer to the charge made on April 13, 1960 by the hon. member that a letter of intent had been sent to Okanagan Helicopter with respect to the aforementioned contract, I wish to re-emphasize that no such letter was ever sent by any official of my department to the Okanagan group or any other group except the one which was going to have the contract. The only letter of intent which was ever sent by this department with respect to this contract was forwarded to Autair Helicopter Services Limited on February 17, 1960. No other letter of intent was sent. Therefore I am doubtful about the source of the information received by the hon. member. It is certainly not reliable as far as this matter is concerned.
The hon. member for Laurier also made a statement to the effect that Pacific Helicopter Services Limited was eliminated because it did not operate a Sikorsky S-55 type of

helicopter. This charge is unfounded. In a letter dated January 6 Pacific Helicopter Services Limited advised the department that they were unable to quote on this type of helicopter service. Therefore the company was not eliminated by officials of my department but they eliminated' themselves, not only with regard to the supplying of the S-55 but also with regard to the Bell G-l or Bell G-2 because, for the efficient operation of the project, it was considered essential that both the Bell and the Sikorsky helicopters be operated by the same company. The quotation submitted by Pacific Helicopter Services Limited for the supplying of two Bells could not, therefore, be considered further.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: If the facts are as stated by the minister, why was Autair allowed to submit a tender when they did not own a Sikorsky S-55 at the time?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
If the hon. member will be patient I think he will get the answer. Let us take one matter at a time.
With regard to the charge that Autair Helicopter Services Limited did not operate the S-55 type of helicopter, I am advised by reliable sources that this is also unfounded. In fact, Autair Helicopter had two S-55 helicopters under operation at that time. Furthermore, this company had only to indicate their interest in supplying this type of helicopter to the department to be considered, as long as we were satisfied under the regulations of the air transport board that they could supply one and that the necessary permission, rates and so forth had been established.
It was also said that Autair's tariffs were not the lowest. The hon. member for Laurier stated in the house on April 13 that "a careful analysis of the sessional paper which the minister tabled in the house, No. 235, tabled on March 25, 1960, indicates that the tariff filed by Autair was not the lowest." I cannot disagree enough with this statement as the sessional paper to which the hon. member referred indicates that Autair's tariffs, based on a utilization of 100 hours per month are clearly the lowest.
The charges made by the hon. member for Laurier to the effect that Autair was not sufficiently qualified to do this type of operation are quite incorrect.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
The air transport board disagrees with you on that.
24. 1960	5383
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
I will deal first with the suggested inability to operate. As the hon. member for Laurier knows, the Department of Transport has very strict safety regulations, and any company that cannot comply at all times with these safety regulations is not allowed to fly. Furthermore, Autair Helicopter Services Limited had two Bell helicopters on location with my department last season in support of survey parties. The survey season of those two parties was a complete success, which is partly accounted for by the efficient support given by the helicopters' operators. It is a fact recognized by officials of my department that when a contract is awarded to a new company the department usually receives far better service because the company goes all out to make a success of its operations.
As far as management ability is concerned, I might also point out to the hon. member that Bristol Aero Industries Limited, which are now owners of Spartan Air Services, have called upon the services of the president of Autair to manage the integrated services of Spartan's and Autair's helicopter services division. The choice of Mr. Connor, the president of Autair, certainly is a reflection of his ability. I might say that I have had no personal contact with Mr. Connor; I do not even know him. I am not here to defend Mr. Connor. The only matter that concerns my department is to be fair to everybody and to assure the best service.
I come now to the department's estimate of 100 hours flying per month per machine, another matter mentioned this morning by the hon. member for Laurier. The hon. member stated in the house on April 13 and again today that our estimate of 100 hours per month per machine flying time was a rather unlikely figure under extreme Arctic weather conditions, and that we had chosen the 100 hour figure to suit Autair's interests. I will simply say that our own departmental estimates, which were considered by treasury board officials some time before December, 1959, were based on a utilization of 100 hours per month per machine.
I should like the hon. member to listen to what I am saying now. To confirm this, may I say that an interim report on the operation of this project indicates that the three machines had accumulated 200.25 hours of flying in a 12-day period from the start of the operation up to and including the 30th of April. If my hon. friend wishes to make a few calculations he will see that if this rate of flying is maintained the basis of 100 hours per month per machine will have been greatly underestimated.
These are the facts as far as I know them, and I am making these statements and giving

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys this information to the committee in all sincerity. In concluding I wish to thank all members who have made contributions to the discussion of my estimates. I am grateful for their constructive suggestions and the officials of my department will certainly take advantage of them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few observations in connection with the reply which the minister has made to the charges and complaints made by myself in connection with this matter earlier during the session and again today. In replying the minister did not make any answer with respect to the request I made that he either investigate this matter or suggest to his colleague, the Minister of Transport, that an investigation should be held. In replying the minister said a great deal about safety regulations and the safe operations of Autair Helicopter.
I am telling the minister, without any fear of contradiction, that the air transport board turned these people down because of, amongst other things, their lack of safety. They had had six accidents in 1959 and they had four accidents in 1960, and their insurance was cancelled. Under those circumstances, how anyone can say that these people were conducting a safe operation, I do not know. Certainly the governmental body responsible for the operation of air carriers felt otherwise and they turned the application down. I am therefore not paying a great deal of attention to what the minister has said in this respect, and of course I say that to him respectfully.
Then the minister has made a great deal of the fact that Pacific Helicopter withdrew or eliminated themselves by saying that they did not possess any S-55 Sikorsky machines. Did the minister or his officers make any attempt to inquire whether Autair Helicopter had any S-55 Sikorsky machines in operation at the time? The minister said they had two. But if the minister looks at the evidence which was given at the hearing before the air transport board and which I have read through carefully he will find that it is clear from this evidence that they did not have any S-55 Sikorsky machines at the time. They may well have leased one or two of them afterwards as a pretext in order to comply with the terms of the contract, but certainly in the evidence which was given before the air transport board, and which I have gone over very carefully, there is not the slightest indication of that situation. I do not think it behooves the officers of the minister's department to determine

this matter; I think it is up to the air transport board. The committee knows what has transpired in so far as this matter is concerned.
Then the minister has stated that Bristol Aero Industries now own Spartan and that they have called on Mr. Connor to manage their operations.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: I have been told that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
That is the point. I asked the Minister of Transport on the orders of the day for a reply to that question and the minister's reply to me was this: the hon. member for Laurier seems to know a great deal more about this matter than I do or than does the air transport board; let him find out from them. Now the minister rises in his place in the chamber and says that is the information he has. The official information from the Minister of Transport certainly is not indicative of that situation. It seems to me that before the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys can say that Bristol have availed themselves of the know-how of Mr. Connor we should at least have a statement from the air transport board because this sale or presumed sale or presumed taking over by Bristol of Autair must be approved by the air transport board. I should like to know whether it has been approved. I think the minister who comes forward and makes a statement such as that which he has made should at least tell us whether or not the air transport board has approved of this and whether or not Mr. Connor is now, because of his great experience, in charge. That will make all the difference in the world. I have grave doubts that such is the case. I cannot imagine in my own mind the air transport board on the one hand turning down Autair because they did not have financial responsibility and on the other hand saying "Put this man Connor in charge of the new operation".
Then something was said about a letter of intent. The minister has made a clear-cut statement that there was no letter of intent. I said originally that upon the information I had at the time there was a letter of intent. If the minister makes the statement that there is not one, I think it is the duty of an hon. member to accept the statement made by the minister in that respect. It may well be that the information I had was erroneous, although that was the information which I gave to the house at the time and which I had every reason to believe was accurate. However, I am not going to enter into a dispute with the minister in so far as that matter is concerned.
As the minister knows, there is more than one way of giving a letter of intent. As the minister knows, sometimes loose language is

used. It may well be that while I was not entirely accurate in the statement I made originally, in effect I am accurate. It may very well be that without any actual letter of intent, what was told to the Okanagan people by word of mouth was that, being the lowest tenderer, they would have the contract. That is certainly the information that was given to me, although not by the Okanagan people. As I said earlier, I have had no communication with any officer of the Okanagan company in connection with the matter.
However, there is unquestionably a doubt about this whole matter. Here a governmental body turns down this company because it is not responsible financially and I have here the order of the board turning it down. On appeal to the minister it is approved. Then the company gets this large contract. Notwithstanding what the minister has said it seems to me that there is on record enough to warrant an investigation. That is all I have asked for. In view of what I have said and in view of what I think raises certainly a grave doubt, I wonder whether the minister would not ask his colleague the Minister of Transport to carry on an investigation so that once and for all we would know whether these complaints and these charges are well founded.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: All I can say about this matter of investigation is that I will discuss the matter with my colleague the Minister of Transport.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: Before the minister leaves that point, may I say this. I think perhaps the minister should go a little bit further than that. If the Minister of Transport is not willing to have an investigation by the air transport board into the matter, will the minister himself give an undertaking that he will see that it is specifically referred to the public accounts committee at the next session of the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: This is not my responsibility, Mr. Chairman, this is the responsibility of the Minister of Transport. When the minister is in the chamber with his estimates I think the matter might be raised again and discussed with him, not with me.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
Has the minister any comment to make with regard to the department's views or its investigation into the question of offshore rights as promulgated by the regulations that were issued by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources with regard to the north? I wonder whether the minister's department has a view or is making any study on this matter
24. 1960	5385
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys because it raises an issue that is likely to be of great interest to some of the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: I understand that this matter is not under the responsibility of my department. However, I will simply do my best and discuss the matter with my colleague, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: I know the matter is not definitely under the department. I do not know that the regulations as issued by the minister's department are really under his department. I imagine they may be open to challenge in the courts on the part of the provinces because, as I said, under the regulations that came out the federal government assumes that it had these offshore rights. I think this matter still has to be settled. I was wondering what interest was being taken in the matter by the minister's department. After all, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is not a department that has been primarily interested, except in the Northwest Territories, in mineral resources of various kinds. I would just hope that we could learn from the minister at some time- and I will be quite wiling to do it by correspondence-what the views of his officials are on this matter and just what consultation took place before what I think is an outright statement of the federal position came out as contained in these regulations.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that these regulations have been promulgated by the minister of northern affairs, I assume the minister also agrees with them as far as his department is concerned. Presumably the minister accepts the position laid down in these regulations, that the ownership of mineral resources at the bed of the sea under territorial waters, and indeed to the extent of the continental shelf, lies in the crown in the right of the federal government. I take it that is the position of the minister and his department on this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, that is the position we take and we have always taken it. The regulations are established by the other department. They are studied and discussed by the officials before they are published.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: Then I would like to make the statement that in the view of our party we think that is as it should be and that these offshore rights should be controlled by and belong to the federal government. However, I am quite aware of the fact that it is open to question and future argument.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
Just one final question. Has any province made any representations to the
5388	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys minister on this issue, because it is not now an issue between the provinces and the federal government?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: No representations have been made to me personally. It might have been the case with the department of northern affairs, I do not know, but not with my department.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister what progress is being made in the problem I raised about nitrogen explosives. What work is the department doing to eliminate that type of explosive and adopt an explosive which would not create this nitrogen gas problem in the mining industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: There is no question of replacing the explosives, but we did make tests to reduce the danger to the public. Does that answer the question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
Every year miners die from the use of this type of explosive. It is not because they get involved in the blast, but they die because of the after effects. I am told there are other substances besides nitrogen which can be used in the manufacture of explosives which does not leave a deadly gas in working areas after they have been used. I understand other forms of material can be used in the mines which will not produce this nitrogen effect. If that is true, I suggest that the department of mines
IMr. Pearson.]

outlaw the use of nitrogen in dynamite and replace it with something which will fill the same need.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: I might say that the use of explosives is not the responsibility of the federal government; it is the responsibility of the province concerned. The services we provide relating to safety are the making of tests in our laboratories which are designed to help advise the provinces of the danger of such and such explosives. But the responsibility of deciding on the kind of explosives to be used belongs to the provinces.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext:
I agree that is probably true but what happens is that the federal government agrees that dynamite must meet certain specific requirements, that it is properly labelled and has proper ingredients. I assume there are inspectors in all the large explosive factories who check the content of the explosives, but what I suggest is that part of the manufacture of explosives entails the use of a lethal material which in the past has killed many people and maimed quite a number of others.
This would appear to me to be the responsibility of the government. If we have a research department which can ascertain the method of making an explosive which does not have this lethal quality, then I think all we have to do to produce this type of powder is to pass a regulation that no nitrogen is to be used. It is true that once the powder is approved and used by the mines, the condition of which I am complaining does not come from the powder itself but from the explosion which takes place. This is the responsibility at the present time of the provincial government under their mine safety regulations. But the basic commodity which the government is approving as acceptable in the manufacture of dynamite is lethal, and if there is a substitute for it, as I understand there is, I think it is the federal government's responsibility to see that this new type of powder is the only powder which should be licensed for use underground or in closed quarters.
I see no reason why the government could not make this type of regulation. We make regulations that you cannot carry dynamite in certain types of trucks without certain protection being provided. I would suggest even more protection in this case because I have never heard of anyone getting into any trouble by improper handling of this material, throwing it around, or that sort of thing. However, a lot of people do get into trouble from this nitrogen gas problem.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: No. I would like to know why the minister is reluctant to insist that his department develops this type of explosive which is not dangerous and why his department continues to licence companies to manufacture dynamite which I consider to be dangerous to health.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORTED STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF ONTARIO ON COMING "FIGHT"
speechtext: I can say this, that this explosive might be safe on the ground but unsafe or dangerous underground. They are two different situations with the same explosive. As I said, we make the tests and all the assays and make our report to the provinces. It is then up to them to forbid this or that explosive in their own regulations. We cannot interfere in that matter. We can have regulations about transportation, but as far as the use of explosives themselves is concerned, the responsibility belongs to the province concerned. If there is any other danger the Criminal Code would come into the picture and it would then be a matter of provincial responsibility. That is why we cannot interfere.

speechtext:
The objectives of the institute are to bring about co-operation and collaboration among the American nations in the conduct of their cartographic, geographic and historical activities and to assist them in their scientific and cultural work in these fields. It serves as a medium for stimulating and co-ordinating these activities and for disseminating information relating to the progress being made within the respective countries.
Since the institute's major fields of activity are surveying and mapping, geography and natural resources, history and anthropology, three commissions are set up within the institute: the commission on cartography, that on geography, and the third on history. The institute comprises 20 member states, and Canada has participated as an observer in all meetings since 1943.
The work of the institute is scientific and technical in nature and does not in any way reflect political attitudes. Canada has since the formation of the institute participated as a welcomed non-member in the sections dealing with cartography and geography. This co-operation has been in the form of reports and advice in dealing with the technical aspects of mapping and geography. The participating member countries of the institute have welcomed this help and the secretariat has consistently urged that Canada become a member. I am pleased to report that Canada has now accepted the invitation to join as a full member of the institute.

Besides providing an opportunity for common discussion of matters relating to cartography, geography and history, our membership in the Pan-American institute of geography and history will assist toward this furthering of co-operation and good will between Canada and the Latin American countries.

maintopic: WABUSH LAKE RAILWAY COMPANY LIMITED AND ARNAUD RAILWAY COMPANY
WABUSH LAKE RAILWAY COMPANY LIMITED AND ARNAUD RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-24, respecting Wabush Lake Railway Company Limited and Arnaud Railway Company.
He said: I wish to give just a brief outline of this bill which deals with the Wabush Railway Company Limited, a Newfoundland railway company, and the Arnaud Railway Company, a Quebec railway company. These two companies are presently subject to the

laws and statutes of their respective province. The purpose of this bill is to bring these companies within the jurisdiction of this parliament and also to give the companies permission to construct a railway from the site of the Wabush Lake Railway Company and the Arnaud Railway Company, if necessary, prior to 1965. The purpose of the railway is to transport concentrate ore products to be produced by Wabush Iron Ore Company Limited from a mine site in Labrador to a point on the St. Lawrence near Seven Islands approximately 290 miles distant. The whole matter involves an investment of about $200 million, of which about $20 million has already been invested. It will cause direct employment for about 2,000 people and naturally it will indirectly result in further numbers being employed. It will also involve the development of a new town site in the location of the mining site. It is hoped that after the mine is in operation it will involve an output of about 10 million tons of low grade ore.
The purpose of this railway is to connect with a railway already developed and known as the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway and hence to transport the products of the mine down to the St. Lawrence. I understand some of the ore is to be delivered to Hamilton.
The arrangement is that the officials of the company will be present at the hearings of the committee which will deal with this bill and they will be able to answer any particular or technical questions that might arise. Those who are interested might go to the committee at that time. However, if hon. members of the house have some questions I might be able to answer them at this time. I understand the hon. member for Laurier has some questions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to deal with the bill which is now before the house, namely Bill No. S-24, respecting Wabush Lake Railway Company Limited and Arnaud Railway Company. I am pleased that the matter has come forward in this fashion, although I cannot say that I am particularly pleased about all of the actions that have gone on so far in connection with the bill. None the less, I think I would be remiss in my duty were I not to say immediately at the outset that those of us who are on this side of the house, will support the bill. We will support it because we think this is a good thing for Canada, and because we feel that the development on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river, partly in the province of Newfoundland and partly in the province 79951-0-3404
Private Bills
of Quebec, will bring about, as the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) has said, an expenditure of some $200 million, $20 million of which have now been either expended or committed.
As I understand it, the project is to link the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company which now exists and which brings iron ore from Knob Lake or Schef-ferville down that company's railway to the St. Lawrence river at the port of Seven Islands. The object of this bill is to tie the two lines to the Quebec Iron Ore Railway Company, namely the Wabush Lake Railway Company at the northern end, which will make the link with the Labrador mine and the Arnaud Railway Company on or very close to the shores of the gulf of the St. Lawrence, which will make the link between the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company and a new port on the St. Lawrence. As the hon. member has said, the intention is to bring these railways under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada and the board of transport commissioners.
But in rising at this time I have another purpose; and I hope the hon. member and those on the other side of the house who have sponsored this bill will not begrudge me the occasion that I intend to take to say a word about, first, the tremendous development that has taken place all along the north shore of the St. Lawrence, thanks to the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. I think it can be said with accuracy and with truth that because of the transportation facilities which have been established and because of the reduction in transportation costs there is great industrial development from the lower St. Lawrence right up to the head of the lakes. I have been told-and I believe this to be true-that more money is being expended upon industrial development because of the opening of the seaway to the commerce of the world than upon the power and navigation facilities themselves.
There is no question in the world that the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway as well as the iron ore development would not have taken place had it not been for the decision of the former government-and I say this to the members of the government now-unanimously, because that attitude was adopted by both sides of the house-which was a good one for Canada. The Iron Ore Company of Canada has a development which I think runs into hundreds of millions of dollars. I may be mistaken in the amount but it is a tremendous one. It consists of the town-site at Schefferville, originally known as Knob Lake, a 360-mile railway built at private cost extending from Knob Lake to Seven Islands; a vast mining operation; and

Private Bills
extensive dock facilities. There has been the development of hangars, warehouses and the like at Seven Islands and it is really the project which broke the back of the opposition to the St. Lawrence seaway. Had it not been for the discovery of iron ore in the fields of Labrador and Quebec I do not think it would have been economically possible to convince the governments of both Canada and the United States that this project should be proceeded with.
The second thing I want to say, and I want to direct this particularly to the attention of those who sit in the government benches, is that it seems to me that the proper advantage is not being taken of this development by the government. It has repeatedly been said, and I believe it is true, that the seaway both from the power and the navigation point of view would aid the development of this country tremendously. That is a fact. But I think it could be helped a great deal more by the development of secondary industries, and I wonder whether the government should not be directing greater attention toward the development of secondary industry all along both shores of the St. Lawrence seaway.
I say this because I have given it a great deal of thought, and I am convinced that those of you who sit in the cabinet benches feel the same way about this matter. It was predicted that there would be, because of this iron ore development large movements in domestic traffic. That is, iron ore traffic that moves from the lower St. Lawrence up to the south shores of lake Ontario and lake Erie; and conversely grain traffic that moves from the head of the lakes to Montreal and other St. Lawrence ports.
That is taking place, but I think because of the development of the common market areas on the continent of Europe greater attention should be paid to the development of secondary industries. In the metropolitan area of Montreal there is a great deal of development going on now. I think that if the federal government in co-operation with the provincial governments and the planning departments of provincial governments was to give consideration to establishment of secondary industries which arise out of developments such as this bill will bring about that would be one way in which to reduce not so much the seasonal unemployment as the cyclical, the business and the technological unemployment which exists in this country at the present time.
Then there are one or two other matters which I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. member, and they are these. I do not think that the Iron Ore Company of

Canada, through its subsidiary Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company, because of the agreements which it has made with the Wabush company, should be placed because of this bill in an inferior position to that in which it was placed prior to the existence of this bill should it be passed by the house. In the other place, in an attempt to meet that position, one amendment was made and I think that consideration should be given to another amendment which should be made to this bill, and that has to do with the rights covered by the agreement between Wabush and Iron Ore. I believe these have to do with rights on the northern end of the project, namely the 40 miles which extend from the Labrador mine to an area south of the Schefferville area. The Iron Ore Company have, I believe, certain perpetual rights because of that agreement.
The hon. member and the house probably know, or we will be told when the bill is brought before the committee, that it may well be that the Iron Ore Company will not be placed in the same position as it was heretofore because of this bill. However, I think this development is going to inure to the benefit of Canada. I believe that any project wherein $200 million is going to be spent for the development of Canadian resources is a good thing and should be approved by all parties in the house, subject to the amendment which I indicated a moment ago.
I think the hon. member should tell us who is the owner of the Wabush railway company and who is the owner of the Arnaud railway company, and whether Canadian Javelin still hold interests in either of those companies.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. Browne (Minister without Portfolio):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly interested in this bill and I am very gratified to learn that the members of the opposition are giving it their support.
I was a member for the Newfoundland legislature when arrangements were made between Canadian Javelin and the Newfoundland government and authority was then given to the Wabush Lake Railway Company Limited. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) has described pretty accurately the position with regard to the railways concerned. The present railway, known as the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company runs from north to south from Seven Islands to Schefferville almost in a straight line, and the two railways concerned here run from east to west, one at a point about 224 miles from Seven Islands and the other one I believe about ten miles from Seven Islands. The lower line runs west along the gulf of St. Lawrence toward the new port

which is going to be created there. The other branch line which runs 40 miles from the main line west to lake Wabush and Carol lake will run to two new mines, one of which is almost ready for operation at Carol lake owned by the Timmins interests, the Hollinger interests and steel companies in the United States. It is hard to say who owns the other one, the lake Wabush development. It was promoted by the Canadian Javelin company and there are a number of steel companies in the United States associated with its development.
The hon. member for Laurier referred to the fact that the St. Lawrence seaway made this development-I do not think he said possible, but certainly made it much more promising than it would have been. It made it much more successful than it would have been because the mines were discovered many years before it was decided to build the seaway. But I believe that even if the seaway had not been built the mines would still have been developed. Certainly the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway has made it a very promising affair and has also given justification for the consideration of secondary industries which the hon. member advocated, some of which I believe have started already.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think what I said was that were it not for the discovery of iron ore in Labrador and Quebec it would not have been possible to build the seaway; it was really the discovery of iron ore which overcame the opposition to the seaway.

I did not
understand that that was the point which the hon. member was making. However, I accept his explanation.
I should like to give credit to the Iron Ore Company for the tremendous development which has been brought to Labrador and Quebec territories which adjoin Labrador. This has been a remarkable development and it is still only at the beginning. The ore at Schefferville and Knob Lake is of high quality. It is even beautiful to look at. Last year I was looking at some of the ore as it was taken out of the mines in Schefferville and Knob Lake, and I was surprised to find that this was so, as I believe, most other hon. members who saw it would be. The other ore at Lake Wabush is ore of a lower grade of iron content, but as a result of benefication processes it has been possible to produce a high grade product which will be shipped along this new railway to the main line and then down to the St. Lawrence.
Those of us who come from Newfoundland have been thinking of using the tremendous power of the Hamilton river in the
Private Bills
neighbourhood of Grand Falls, and it is certainly pleasant news that the Brinco people-the British Newfoundland Corporation-have already begun the construction of a power plant with an initial development of
120,000	horsepower. But when we remember that this great river is capable of developing over eight million horsepower we can see that there are further possibilities for the utilization of this great natural resource for the refining of ore in one way or another whether by the construction of blast furnaces or in other ways. This great source of power may also be used to bring power to sites along the St. Lawrence river where some of the secondary industries mentioned will be established.
I am certainly glad that this measure is going through and that it receives the approval of hon. members of the opposition. I am sure the sponsor of the bill will be pleased to answer any other questions in connection with it.

After surveying the record of the proceedings in the other place it is apparent that there is some kind of principle of government ownership involved in the problem of the Wabush railway. In fact, the railway as it exists now is not so much a railway as an extension of the Iron Ore Company's facilities and this will probably come to an end when the railway becomes geared to handle ore from the other company or perhaps from two other companies. This, in our view, is in many ways as it should be. While one could compliment the Iron Ore Company of Canada for its imagination in creating this line, the fact is that this is a major communication using the public land of Canada though in this case it is under provincial jurisdiction. Through this bill the whole enterprise as a transport medium comes within the orbit of the federal government and the board of transport commissioners. To that extent the people are given more control and a wider interest in the operation.
One can understand the reason why the Iron Ore Company of Canada was not too pleased about this particular development- I have taken that view of the company's attitude after reading the cross-examination- and I am certain that from a business point of view one might have great sympathy with the company's position. But at the moment unless we go forward with the bill as it is- and I cannot really see the value of making amendments-we should be placing the Wabush group and the other group associated with them in the branch line which is going to be constructed in a position where they would not have any bargaining strength as

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a short statement to make regarding the dominion coal board estimates. Hon. members will agree, I think, that a long statement would

be inappropriate at this time while all of us are looking forward to the report of the royal commission on coal.
Let me deal first with policy. From the long range point of view the government's policy is simply to keep a sympathetic and open mind until the information, the conclusions and the recommendations of the Rand report are available for study.
But a short range policy is necessary. This is positive, clear, easily understood and practical. It is simply to improve the present situation wherever we can-and if the situation cannot be improved, then to maintain it without deterioration-until the Rand report is ready and long range policy can be formulated.
The dominion coal board estimates have been prepared from this policy background. It is essentially the same policy that reduced to normal proportions the huge stockpiles of coal at Sydney and Montreal, held unemployment in Cape Breton to a minimum when mass unemployment was threatened, restored a good measure of coal mining employment in the Crowsnest pass area of British Columbia and Alberta and is currently staving off suggested mine closures in Nova Scotia.
This is a good record by comparison with other countries which are experiencing crisis conditions in their coal industries. I understand that 25,000 miners are unemployed in one small European country. There are huge stockpiles of unsold coal at nearly all European coal mines. Last year while our Canadian stockpiles were being reduced to normal the undistributed stockpiles in the United Kingdom grew by 10 million tons and now contain 32 million tons of coal.
Any review of the current coal situation in Canada has to begin with the fact that coal consumption in this country is still declining under the competitive impact of oil and natural gas. The total Canadian consumption of coal in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1960 was 23,758,621 tons. This was a decrease of 1,650,000 tons by comparison with total consumption in the previous year. Viewed, however, against the more than four million ton drop in consumption which occurred in 1958-59, it can perhaps be regarded as a levelling off of the downward trend.
One item in the consumption figures deserves a historical footnote. I refer to the railway consumption of coal. Last year it was only 895,000 tons. The footnote for history is the fact that railway locomotives in this country once burned 13 million tons of coal annually.
Another item in the consumption figures is of interest. Coke and gas plants used
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys nearly one million more tons of coal last year than in the previous year, a reflection of the high level of activity in our steel industry.
On the production side, Canadian mines produced 10,870,000 tons of coal during the year ended March 31. This was a decrease of
300.000	tons by comparison with the previous year but again it was a reduction of the decline by comparison with the year before last. One has the feeling that, if it were not for the intense new competition of natural gas and residual oil, the worst period would now be over for coal; that the upswing, so long predicted by the economists, would be about to begin.
Nova Scotia coal production in 1959-60 was 162,500 tons greater than in 1958-59 and New Brunswick production was 88,700 tons greater. The other coal regions produced somewhat lower tonnages last year than the year before, with the greatest decrease,
356.000	tons, occurring in Saskatchewan.
The Saskatchewan decrease is probably
less a reflection of contracted demand than of disrupted production by a fire at one of the large mines in the Estevan district. As a matter of fact, Saskatchewan and New Brunswick are the two regions where the coal industry can be said to be in a definitely healthy condition. We have reports that Saskatchewan lignite has been able to hold its markets fairly successfully against low cost natural gas.
Little that is encouraging can be said about the household market for Alberta's subbituminous coal. Its use continues to decline as more and more homes throughout the prairie provinces are converted to oil and natural gas.
Here is a case where the hard fact must be faced that increased subventions or any other measure within federal jurisdiction would be powerless to maintain this sector of the Alberta industry. All but a few tons of the markets that are being lost are in the west itself. For some of Alberta's sub-bituminous coal there is a future in thermal electric power generation; but this is small comfort to the miners who have produced the coal for the prairie household market and now see employment diminishing. The coal for thermal power will be mined by strip methods.
I have already mentioned the Crowsnest pass area of Alberta and British Columbia. The greatly improved situation in that district is the result of increased export subvention assistance combined with the sustained efforts of the coal board and the producers to interest the Japanese steel industry in our western coking coals. About a year
5398	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys ago, you will remember, Mr. Chairman, a Canadian coal mission visited Japan with excellent results. During the 1959-60 fiscal year 263,541 tons of Alberta and British Columbia coal were exported to that country.
The coal board followed up its efforts of last year by arranging with the fuels and mining practise division of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to carry out extensive research on blends of Japanese and Canadian coals. The board then borrowed two specialists from mines and technical surveys, one an expert on coke production, the other an expert on steel making, and sent them to Japan to hold discussions and exchange information with the technical experts of all the major Japanese steel companies. It was the first such technical mission ever sent by any of the numerous countries which sell coal to Japan. The Japanese have been genuinely appreciative of our attempt to determine scientifically how Canadian coals can best meet the special requirements of their growing steel industry. This year the Japanese importers have already placed firm orders for half a million tons of Canadian coal. These favourable export developments could not be fully foreseen when the main estimates were prepared. At a later date I shall present to you a supplementary estimate of the subvention funds needed for this additional tonnage.
The Nova Scotia situation is known to all of us. You are aware, Mr. Chairman, of what we have been doing to maintain the Nova Scotia industry and keep unemployment among the Cape Breton miners to a minimum while awaiting the report which, we hope, will point the way to fundamental solutions for the industry's problems.
Using the increased subvention funds which you approved last year, combined with the special contribution of the provincial government of Nova Scotia and combined also with a tremendous sales effort, much of it conducted personally by the chairman of the coal board, we squeezed a substantial tonnage of Nova Scotia coal into the Ontario market. We did this while the Ontario market has been so contracted that it has been buying approximately 4,500,000 tons less United States coal. We additionally succeeded in maintaining, to a considerable degree, the traditional Nova Scotia coal markets in the province of Quebec against the competition of natural gas, residual oil and surplus hydroelectric power.
The Nova Scotia government has asked us to continue this high emergency level of assistance during the 1960-61 fiscal year, again offering to make a contribution of up to $500,000 to the increased cost, and we have agreed to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this stage in the discussion of estimates, I simply want to say a few words in connection with the coal mining industry. I am speaking as a layman, but I would like to express some general ideas and make one or two suggestions which, I think, are of some interest.
Coal is obviously one of our most versatile natural underground resources. It can be used in hundreds of ways other than a source of energy. It has been said that North America has about 40 per cent of all the coal in the world, and to give an idea of the importance of coal as a natural resource, experts state that, even if present production were doubled, we would have coal for perhaps a thousand years. That shows the abundance in this country of that recuperable wealth which can be used for years and years to come.
As the minister suggested a few moments ago, there is now heavy unemployment in the coal mining industry, and all experts and specialists in the matter agree that the next ten years will be the hardest. However, the prospects are that, in 15 or 20 years, large scale production will be resumed. Present conditions are due to several causes. The minister mentioned a few of them, like the dieselization program of our railway systems, which has certainly been a blow for our coal industry. We also may say today that, with regard to other sources of energy, prices have remained stable, while in the coal mining industry, prices have increased for several reasons.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, these last few years, we have found new sources of energy, such as natural gas, but we can already see that those sources are not as plentiful as coal and the time will come when we will just have to go back to mining coal

on a high scale. For that reason, I should like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois).
If we expect to have to go back to intensive coal mining say in ten years, why do we not start at once stockpiling coal, to help out that industry and provide jobs for miners? Why, for instance, should we not intensify present production and stockpile coal in various places that could extend, let us say, from eastern Canada to Montreal? I presume that, in case of war, several other sources of energy could become exhausted or rendered unusable; coal so stored would constitute a reserve that could be readily used. I would therefore ask the minister to consider the possibility of stockpiling coal at various places in Canada; that would allow us to accelerate production in our coal mines.
This I think, is a suggestion which deserves to be seriously considered since, I repeat, experts agree that coal production will cease to be a problem 10 or 15 years hence. However, the problem now exists, and I think that if the government seriously considered this suggestion, it would be much easier, during the next ten years, to stabilize that industry which promises to be one of our most important resources in coming years.
Now I have little to add to what I have already said. However, I would also ask the minister to consider raising the amount provided for research on coal uses. I have been reading various articles from the United States and elsewhere, dealing with new processes, permitting the use of coal for a number of purposes, indeed for hundreds of purposes.
I think we in Canada should constantly keep abreast of research being carried out in other countries, so as to be up-to-date and thus help the coal industry, which I think is one of the most important and most promising of our industries.
In closing my remarks, I should like to subscribe to what the minister said about the officers of his department, and particularly those who are in front of his desk. I want them to know we appreciate the magnificent job they are doing and we think that with their know-how, we should be able to give that industry a new lease on life as it cannot be allowed to remain in its present state of stagnation.
I think we should take bold steps to insure that this industry will recover its former activity, for let us not forget that within

maintopic: CORNWALL HIGH LEVEL BRIDGE-GLACIAL TILL CONDITIONS

speechtext:
1.	Did the St. Lawrence seaway authority receive a report or letter from the contractors working

Questions
on the substructure for the Cornwall high level bridge, regarding a difference they found re soil or glacial till conditions as compared to information supplied to them by the authority from previous test borings carried out by the United States corps of engineers or the St. Lawrence seaway authority?
2.	If so, what was the date of the communication, and what was its nature?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister
of Transport):
The St. Lawrence seaway authority advises as follows:
1.	Yes, but subsequent investigations and construction operations disclosed the fallacy of their allegations.
2.	By letter dated January 4, 1957, the contractor stated that in drilling and blasting on the sites of the main piers to loosen material so as to facilitate the driving of steel sheet pile cofferdams and the excavation therein, the material on the Canadian side was found to be dense, glacial till with all kinds of boulders, as expected, and they anticipated no trouble to get a satisfactory bearing for the concrete piers, but that on the United States side the material seemed much softer and did not require any blasting. They expressed the fear that they might need longer penetration of the sheet piling on the United States side and suggested that excavation be carried to a lesser depth than specified and that tubular pipes be driven, as bearing piles, to rock.
N.B.-Consequent to the receipt of this letter the authority had further borings made which confirmed the findings of the U.S. army corps of engineers that the material on the United State side comprised a dense glacial till as found on the Canadian side, except that it was overlain in part by relatively loose gravel and boulders. This indicated no need for a change in design.
By letter dated July 4, 1957, the contractor again made reference to the drilling and blasting of the previous December at which time they "found the Canadian side very hard, the United States side very soft" but that in driving their H-pile falsework in the spring they "could not possibly drive through or dig the Canadian side and the United States side". They were at a loss to explain the December conclusions and questioned if they had been properly located on the United States side. The main feature of this letter, however, was a complaint that the authority had restricted the drilling and pre-blasting on the site of the main piers to elevation 114, three feet above the elevation to which excavation was specified and in consequence of this they could not guarantee excavation to elevation 111 nor could they guarantee that the steel piling in the cofferdams would have enough penetration.
N.B.-Subsequent operations, following drilling and pre-blasting disclosed that the till on both the Canadian and United States sides was so dense that the consulting engineers agreed to the founding of the piers from one to two feet above the specified elevation 111. The nature of the material excavated from within the caissons was the same as that described on the contract plans.

Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of
Transport):
The St. Lawrence seaway authority advises as follows:
1.	The initial survey control system for substructure construction was continued and expanded to cover the precise checking of possible movements of the piers.
2.	(a) Prior to commencement of construction.
(b)	Division engineer.
(c)	General instructions from engineer of construction applicable to all construction work.
(d)	Routine checks, as necessary, throughout the period of construction and until stability of the structure was assured.
(e)	Main piers:
A comparison of elevations taken on December 20, 1957, with elevations previously taken at four points on the top of easterly shaft of pier No. 12 indicates uneven settlement with a maximum differential of about one quarter inch between two diametrically opposite sides. This would suggest tilting of the shaft which would cause a horizontal movement of the top. As there was no apparent horizontal movement of the top of the pier, and as there has been no further evidence of settlement, it has been concluded that the first observations must have been in error. There was no further suggestion of movement in this shaft or any evidence of movement in other shafts.
Cable-bent pier No. 13 (Canadian side):
Initial movement observed to be: Top of west shaft-easterly one eighth inch and southerly one half inch. Top of east shaft- westerly one half inch, and southerly one inch. There has been no vertical settlement or

further horizontal movement. It is believed that the displacements were caused by abnormal forces resulting from the temporary support of construction equipment used in placing parts of the superstructure.
North abutment (Canadian side):
Initial movement observed to be one and one half inch southerly, at the top. There has been no vertical settlement or further horizontal movement.
